Use standard area formulas in terms of R: an equilateral triangle with circumradius R has area S = 3√3 R^2/4; a regular hexagon with circumradius R has area H = 3√3 R^2/2; an equilateral triangle with inradius R has area L = 3√3 R^2. Then compute H^2 and LS and verify they are equal, giving H = √(LS) since areas are positive.

method.method_draft: Read the image first as showing the small triangle and the regular hexagon inscribed in the same circle, with the circle itself tangent to the sides of the large equilateral triangle. From the text, identify the three desired areas L, S, and H. Use only area ratios. Let the circle radius be R. For equilateral triangles, circumradius is twice inradius. The large triangle has inradius R, so its circumradius is 2R, while the small triangle has circumradius R; therefore the large and small equilateral triangles have linear scale ratio 2 and area ratio L:S = 4:1. Next compare the hexagon with the small triangle: the inscribed regular hexagon splits into 6 congruent equilateral triangles of side R, while the inscribed equilateral triangle has the same area as the alternate-vertex triangle in that hexagon, equal to 3 of those small equilateral pieces. Thus H:S = 2:1. Hence L = 4S and H = 2S, so H^2 = 4S^2 = LS, giving H = √(LS).
